extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of public relations and mass communication
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and apply the elements, effects, and audience/public-opinion criteria from a mass communication/public relations textbook chapter to guide strategic communication planning and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source (Sender) characteristics / credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Characteristics of message sources affect receivers’ initial acceptance of the message; source credibility (status, reliability, expertness) amplifies the value of information and contributes a weight factor in the communication process. The sleeper effect describes a long-term source impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use highly credible sources (e.g., recognized medical authorities) to increase initial believability; recognize that source effects vary by situation, topic, and time; the three credibility characteristics multiply to yield source weight. Example: safe-sex messages are more accepted when presented by credible medical authorities than peers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Message characteristics and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Message features influence impact but meanings reside in receivers, so the same message may be interpreted differently by different people; message effects are mediated by receiver factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design messages knowing audiences will interpret differently; anticipate mediated effects (obstinate audience) rather than expecting simple cause-effect; tailor content to target publics and their interpretive frames.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium/channel selection
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of medium (face-to-face, email, broadcast, digital, etc.) affects the nature, immediacy, senses engaged, feedback, and costs of communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer interpersonal (face-to-face) for direct, powerful exchanges with immediate feedback when appropriate; use mediated channels to extend time/distance or reduce cost; understand media effects when choosing single or multiple media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receiver (Audience) activity and segmentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiences are active, not passive; individual differences (group membership values, aggressiveness, self-esteem) influence susceptibility to persuasion; targeting specific and well-defined publics is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment audiences and target messages to specific publics; consider receivers' group identities and psychological traits to predict receptivity; encourage audience involvement and interpersonal discussion to amplify effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship context dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Relational communication reflects four basic dimensions: (1) emotional arousal, composure, and formality; (2) intimacy and similarity; (3) immediacy or liking; and (4) dominance–submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the relationship context (including nonverbal cues like proximity, smiling, touch, eye contact) and cultural differences when crafting and delivering messages; consider how these dimensions shape expectations and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonverbal behavior and cultural differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonverbal behaviors (proximity, smiling, touching, eye contact) communicate intimacy, trust, dominance, persuasiveness, and can be interpreted differently across cultures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for cultural norms (e.g., eye contact taboo in some cultures) when using nonverbal strategies; use nonverbal cues to reduce uncertainty and build relational predictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social environment / systems perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication occurs within social systems (families, groups, organizations) that both produce and are produced by communication; forces in the larger society condition communicators' approaches and audience responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze the broader social context and systemic interdependencies when planning communication; recognize that organizational and societal forces shape message goals and outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group communication factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Group communication depends on the nature of the group (primary/secondary, formal/informal, task/experiential), member characteristics, group size, structure, cohesiveness, and purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor communication strategies to group type and structure; leverage group cohesiveness and appropriate structures to facilitate desired group outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Successful group decision-making tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective group decision making requires (1) an adequate and accurate assessment of the problem, (2) a shared and complete understanding of the goal and success criteria, (3) agreement on positive outcomes, and (4) agreement on negative outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure group communications support these four tasks (information gathering, goal alignment, pros/cons agreement) to improve decision effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation of perceptions / Lippmann's triangular model
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass media help create 'pictures in our heads'—media lie between the scene of action and audience perceptions, shaping how people perceive events, people, and places they cannot directly experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize media's role in constructing public perceptions; manage media representations to influence audience cognitions and subsequent responses to the scene of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivation effects (mean world syndrome)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heavy exposure to certain media (e.g., television) cultivates a shared social reality among viewers, altering perceptions of the world (e.g., perceiving the world as more dangerous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider cumulative, collective media exposure effects on audience worldviews rather than only individual, immediate effects when planning long-term communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agenda-setting theory (first-level)
rubrics_metrics.description: Media influence what audiences think about: relative media emphasis on issues causes corresponding prominence on the public agenda; repetition moves issues from press agenda to public agenda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repeated media exposure to raise issue salience; monitor media emphasis to anticipate public priorities and reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-level agenda-setting / framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Media influence not only what to think about but how to think about it and thereby affect cognitions and predispositions (i.e., second-level agenda-setting or framing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame issues strategically to influence public predispositions and interpretations, not just awareness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue salience (agenda-setting concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: Issue salience determines prominence and penetration of an issue with an audience; frequency of discussion is the largest predictor of salience; interpersonal communication can enhance or interfere with media agenda-setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increase frequency and visibility of messages to boost salience; engage interpersonal channels to reinforce media effects or to counter conflicting media content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive priming (agenda-setting concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior or personal exposure to an issue stimulates interest in media coverage of that issue, enhancing agenda-setting effects even when audiences have some personal experience with the issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage existing personal connections or prior exposures to prime audiences for media messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agenda-building (who builds the media agenda)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agenda-building examines who shapes the media's agenda; research shows actors such as politicians, elected officials, and public relations practitioners are typical agenda builders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize PR's role as an active agenda builder; coordinate with influencers and institutional actors to shape media coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diffusion of innovation adoption criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Innovations are more readily adopted if they are (1) more advantageous than current situation, (2) compatible with prior experience and context, (3) simple, (4) easily tried, and (5) observable with apparent outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When promoting innovations, emphasize relative advantage, compatibility, simplicity, trialability, and observable results; target adopter categories (innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority, laggards) and opinion leaders to speed diffusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of opinion leaders and multistep flow in diffusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinion leaders often acquire information from media and then influence others; the two-step flow model has evolved into multistep flow with many actors and steps affecting adoption decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and engage opinion leaders as intermediaries; design strategies for multi-step diffusion through social networks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spiral of silence (social support and expression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals who perceive their opinion conflicts with majority views tend to remain silent; perceptions of shared support or growing numbers encourage expression; media coverage can reflect, enforce, or challenge these spirals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design campaigns to break spirals of silence (e.g., public information campaigns addressing domestic violence) by visualizing or amplifying social support to encourage expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sociocultural model of persuasion (appearance of consensus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Media messages can provide the appearance of consensus regarding orientation and action, influencing perceptions of social approval/disapproval and thus persuasive outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how media portrayals create perceived consensus and use that to either challenge or reinforce public norms and behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion dimension: Direction
rubrics_metrics.description: Direction indicates the evaluative quality of an opinion (positive–negative; for–against–undecided) and is the most basic, frequently used measure in polling and media reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use direction measures (percentages for/against) for basic snapshots of public stance but recognize their limits for depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion dimension: Intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: Intensity measures how strongly people feel about their opinions, often measured with scaled responses (e.g., 1–10 or strongly disagree to strongly agree).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report intensity alongside direction to understand how deeply opinions are held and to anticipate mobilization or polarization potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion dimension: Stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Stability refers to how long respondents hold the same direction and intensity; measuring stability requires observations at multiple points in time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track opinions over time to assess reactivity to events and the durability of persuasion or attitude change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion dimension: Informational support
rubrics_metrics.description: Informational support measures how much knowledge people hold about the object of their opinion; better-informed individuals may form stronger opinions and act (vote/contact officials) but direction can be unpredictable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess informational depth behind opinions; if informational support is low, consider educational campaigns framed to affected stakeholders to influence direction/intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion dimension: Social support
rubrics_metrics.description: Social support measures the extent to which people think their opinions are shared by others in their social milieu and reflects perceived consensus, which affects willingness to express views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure perceived social support to understand expression dynamics (spiral of silence) and design interventions that alter perceived norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-person effect
rubrics_metrics.description: People tend to underestimate media impact on themselves and overestimate its impact on others, which can influence policy preferences and campaign strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for third-person perceptions when predicting public demands for protective policy or when designing persuasive appeals that rely on perceived vulnerability of others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual orientation components: salience and pertinence
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual orientation toward an object comes from (1) salience — feelings derived from past experiences (what individuals bring to a situation) — and (2) pertinence — relative value based on comparisons in the current situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure both salience (cross-situational predispositions) and pertinence (situation-dependent value) to fully understand individual opinion formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attitudinal system components
rubrics_metrics.description: An attitudinal system comprises four components: (1) evaluative frames of reference (values and interests), (2) cognition (knowledge and beliefs), (3) affection (feelings), and (4) conation (behavioral intentions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When diagnosing or influencing attitudes, attend to all four components rather than focusing on affect alone; tailor messages to shift values, knowledge, feelings, or intended behaviors as appropriate.
